items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to cardiovascular technologists
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S3570

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the public health law, in relation
to cardiovascular technologists

 PURPOSE :

Authorize Cardiovascular Technologists (CVTs) to administer contrast
materials during cardiovascular interventional procedures, under the
direct supervision of a physician.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 defines a cardiovascular technologist

Section 2 authorizes the cardiovascular technologist to administer the
contrast materials during cardiovascular interventional procedures
under the direct supervision of a physician.

Section 3 provides that the bill would take effect immediately

 EXISTING LAW :

Under current law, the contract materials must be administered by
physicians.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Contrast materials are used to improve images produced by x-rays,
computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance (MR) imaging, and
ultrasound. For cardio-vascular procedures the most common contrast
material is a non-ionic radiopaque contrast medium, which is used to
enhance fluoroscopy or cineradiography (moving x-rays). It is
introduced into a patient's artery by inserting a syringe with the
contrast material into a line placed by the physician. When
administered in this manner during a cardiovascular procedure, the
contrast material allows the physician to locate and visualize the
targeted sites in real time. These contrast materials are safe drugs;
mild adverse reactions can occur but are uncommon and treatable.

CVTs assist in technical procedures for cardiac catheterizations and
interventions. Their tasks include patient preparation, assisting
physicians, hemodynamic monitoring, vascular access site management
and first assistant. They must also accurately complete required
documentation for procedures. Their work during cardiovascular
interventions is strictly under a physician's direct supervision.
While CVTs may possess a certification in their field from a college
program, there is no license or certification requirement to be a CVT;
rather, hospitals ensure that CVTs have the knowledge, training and
competency to perform these tasks. CVTs are willing and fully able to
administer contrast materials to patients during cardiovascular
interventional procedures, under the supervision of a physician.

In New York, CVTs are not permitted to administer contrast materials.
The NYS Nurse Practice Act defines the scope of nursing practice and
prohibits others who do not have a nursing license or other relevant
license from engaging in the practice of nursing. In 2006, the Office
of the Professions of the NYS State Education Department issued a
"Practice Alert and Guidelines" that warned against the administration
of medications by unlicensed persons. This prohibition would include
the administration of contrast materials by CVTs. Based on this
ruling, the Department of Health has taken action against hospitals
that have permitted CVTs to administer contrast materials.

The administration of contrast materials by a CVT under the
supervision of a physician raises no significant safety issue. The
medication itself is quite safe. And the setting provides optimal
oversight - during a cardiovascular procedure a physician, nurse, and
other health care professionals are present and monitoring the
procedure. It is a highly controlled environment. In fact, empowering
CVTs to perform this function will improve patient safety by
eliminating the distraction caused when a physician or nurse is pulled
away from more pressing tasks to administer contrast material.  The
use of CVTs is also inherently more cost effective than reliance upon
physicians or nurses for this function.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

New Bill

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

To be determined

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This Act shall take effect immediately
